activities.caption: wish or requirement? file each claim
activities.name: reqWishSort

config.prompt: Wish or requirement? File each claim:

items.label: Search results return within 300 milliseconds at the 95th percentile with 10,000 concurrent users
The service survives the loss of one data centre with under 60 seconds of interruption
REQ-104: The system shall reject a duplicate invoice number within the same fiscal period

config.why: If you cannot write the test that fails, you have not written a requirement — and the disagreement surfaces at acceptance testing, the most expensive possible moment.

activities.caption: pair each technique with what it gets you
activities.name: reqElicitMatch

config.prompt: Pair each method with what it gets you:

pairs.right: actual ones — workarounds, sticky notes, shadow spreadsheets
conflicting stakeholders in one room, conflicts visible early
reactions to something concrete — more reliable than speculation about the abstract
usually the loudest stakeholder wanting more features

config.why: Real users often want less software that fits the work — and each workaround observed is an unmet requirement wearing a disguise.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the elicitor's job
activities.name: reqTranscribeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Users routinely cannot articulate what they need.
They forget the obvious and mis-predict their own behaviour.
The stated wish and the actual need diverge reliably.
So the elicitor's job is dictation: write down the list and build it.
That is why watching nurses chart beats asking nurses to describe charting.
config.correction: The job is closer to diagnosis than dictation — which is why observation and prototyping are first-class techniques.
config.why: Users mis-predict their own behaviour; the divergence is what observation and prototypes exist to catch.

activities.anchor: A hospital booking system gives a compact example
activities.caption: walk the conflict to its resolution
activities.name: reqConflictBranch

config.root: One screen, three legitimate demands. Walk the negotiation:

start.text: Clinicians want full details visible in one click. Administrators object — why?

choices.label: Access must be gated by role for privacy compliance

mis1.text: Not the lesson's conflict — the objection is compliance, not keyboard speed.

n2.text: Patients then demand their own data be visible. Which demand is that?

mis2.text: The demand is transparency — seeing your own data — not throughput.

n3.text: All three are legitimate; some cannot be fully satisfied simultaneously. What resolves them?

choices.label: Read-only summary views, audit logs, granular consent — a negotiated specification
The project manager picks a winner and moves on

mis3.text: A specification that hides the conflict simply schedules the same argument for a later, more expensive date.

end.text: The negotiation is requirements engineering, not politics.

config.why: Surfacing conflicts early is the point — a hidden conflict is an expensive appointment.

activities.anchor: not every elicited wish can be built
activities.caption: fill the four-word scheme
activities.name: reqMoscowCloze

config.text: The workhorse scheme runs: %%0%% — the release fails without it; %%1%% — important but deferrable; %%2%% — nice if cheap; %%3%% — not this time, and we are saying so on the record.
config.hint: Four words, four levels of commitment — the last is the cheapest conflict-prevention device in the field.

activities.caption: true or false — the undersold kind
activities.name: reqQualityJudge

statements.why: These requirements are frequently the binding constraints on the entire design.

statements.s: They constrain every function at once rather than attaching to any single one.
statements.why: Which is why they are adverbs and adjectives, not verbs.

statements.s: A payments system with a perfect feature set that leaks card numbers has failed completely.
statements.why: The quality attribute was the binding one.

statements.s: Some methodologists prefer the label 'quality attribute requirements'.
statements.why: Because the standard label undersells them.

activities.anchor: the field has converged on a spectrum
activities.caption: drag between the two formats
activities.name: reqFormatsCompare

before.label: SRS
before.text: numbered, unique, traceable statements (each clause maps to a test) — beloved of regulated industries because every clause can be audited.

after.label: User story
after.text: 'As a customer, I want a refund button so that I can return damaged goods without calling support' — made rigorous by acceptance criteria; trades completeness for adaptability.

config.why: The story format works when the team can talk to users continuously, and fails silently when it cannot.

activities.anchor: Barry Boehm's studies in the 1970s and 1980s
activities.caption: estimate the per-phase cost growth
activities.name: reqBoehmEstimate

config.prompt: By roughly what multiple does the cost of fixing a requirements defect grow per phase?
config.why: Roughly an order of magnitude per phase — a workshop conversation; weeks in integration; releases, data migrations, emergency patches and trust in production.
